tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (arXiv 2103.00858, published as PVLDB 15(11):2679-2691, 2022, DOI 10.14778/3551793.3551823) benchmarks CARMI against STX B+ Tree and ALEX and, on the SOSD platform, against RMI/RS/ALEX/FAST/ART/B+Tree etc. The CPU (AMD Ryzen 3700X) is stated and the code is public (embryo-labs/CARMI src/ with bundled stx_btree and alex), but no compiler or flags are given, so it cannot be A.

corrections.workload: 7 datasets: 4 synthetic (lognormal, uniform, normal, exponential; 1GB each of <double,double> pairs) plus YCSB, OSMC and Facebook (67,108,864 records each). Workloads: read-only, write-heavy (50/50), read-heavy (95/5), write-partial (85% reads / 15% inserts concentrated in 60-90% of key range) and range scan, with uniform and Zipfian access; single-threaded, 100,000 operations per workload. Plus SOSD: amzn/face/wiki/osmc real-world datasets of 200M 32/64-bit keys, 10M uniform lookups.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Average 2.2x (up to 4.2x) speedup vs STX B+ Tree and 1.9x (up to 7.2x) vs ALEX, using ~0.77x the memory of the B+ Tree; on the SOSD platform the average speedup over the nearest competitor, RMI, is 1.2x (1.21x, up to 1.5x). In SOSD Table 3, ART is slightly faster on face32 (182.36 vs 187.43 ns) and RMI/RS are within ~1-5 ns on face64/wiki.
corrections.caveats: Very low adoption (10 stars) and the repo has not been updated since Jan 2022. Numbers are the authors' own, from a peer-reviewed PVLDB 2022 paper. The abstract's 'outperforms all baselines on SOSD' is slightly overstated: ART beats CARMI on face32 and RMI is effectively tied on face64. No compiler or flags are stated. The lambda parameter is tuned per dataset.

notes: The abstract numbers match the record. The workload's '~10^8 keys' was wrong: real datasets have 67,108,864 records, and the 10^8 in the paper is a key-value multiplier for the synthetic data. GitHub metadata was verified: MIT, 10 stars, not a fork, last commit 2022-01-03, so abandoned is correct.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 13(8) 2020 paper compares PGM-index against the STX B+-tree v0.9, the authors' CSS-tree and a 2-stage RMI, and reports the 874 MiB vs 87 KiB and 341 MiB vs 4 MiB (82.7x) figures. The CPU is only '2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold' (no model) and no compiler or flags are given, so it cannot be A.

corrections.baseline: STX B+-tree (v0.9) and cache-efficient CSS-tree (authors' implementation), plus a 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Static: PGM-index matches the fastest STX B+-tree's query latency using ~10,000x less space (87 KiB vs 874 MiB, 'four orders of magnitude') and matches the fastest CSS-tree using 82.7x less space (4 MiB vs 341 MiB); it dominates the 2-stage RMI in the space-time trade-off (RMI MAE 892±3729 vs 226±139 for PGM; RMI built 14.5x slower). Dynamic: the Dynamic PGM-index was 13-71% faster than the STX B+-tree for most query/update mixes (1.0% and 15.2% slower at 0.8 and 0.9 query fractions), using 611-3891x less space.
corrections.caveats: The VLDB'20 paper states only '2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold' (no model), with no compiler or flags. The static comparisons against the B+-tree and CSS-tree are same-speed at far less space rather than strictly faster. The strictly-faster wins are against RMI and, in the dynamic setting, 13-71% over the STX B+-tree on most (not all) workload mixes. All numbers come from the authors' own experiments.

notes: The claimed numbers appear verbatim in the paper (Sections 7.2 and 7.3). I added the dynamic-PGM 13-71% latency win over the STX B+-tree, a genuine speed claim the record missed. GitHub metadata was verified: Apache-2.0, 874 stars, not a fork, last commit 2024-11-28, so stale is correct.

tier_reason: First-party README table (picobench) compares art::art against std::map and std::unordered_map. The benchmark code is public (bench/*.cpp, run via 'make release && make bench'; CMake Release flags -O3 -DNDEBUG), but no compiler, CPU or stdlib is stated, so it is C.

corrections.workload: 1.6M operations per benchmark (picobench Dim=1,600,000) with sparse keys: random mt19937_64 64-bit values formatted as decimal strings via std::to_string. Covers delete, insert, mixed, query uniform, query uniform (base-64 keys) and query Zipf, comparing art::art vs std::map<std::string,...> vs std::unordered_map<std::string,...>.
corrections.claimed_speedup: ~1.5x-2.4x faster than std::map: delete 1.985x, insert 2.118x, mixed 1.824x, query-uniform 1.517x, query-uniform base-64 keys 2.390x, query-zipf 1.817x. Against std::unordered_map, ART is slower on delete (0.691), query-uniform (0.518), query-uniform base-64 (0.655) and mixed (0.928), and at parity on insert (1.029) and query-zipf (1.005).
corrections.caveats: First-party micro-benchmark (picobench harness, not nanobench). No compiler, stdlib or CPU is stated, and the numbers were added to the README in 2018. The README heading says '16M keys' but the table shows 1.6M. Keys are std::to_string'd random 64-bit ints, so the baseline is std::map<std::string>, and to_string cost sits inside every timed loop. The hashmap benchmark uses a random_device seed while ART and std::map use a fixed seed. GPL-3.0 license.

notes: The numbers match the README table, but the record left out the 2.39x base-64-keys row and mislabeled the key type and harness. I cleared baseline_stdlib because the README never says which standard library was used (Linux/GCC libstdc++ is likely but unverified). GitHub metadata was verified: GPL-3.0, 174 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-11-24, so active is correct.
